DLCO falling below 40 % predicted is a red flag for impending respiratory failure and is often asked as a trigger for referral for lung transplantation (rare in Kenya but conceptually important).
Giving reassurance without arranging review when a red flag is present.
Refer early for dialysis if the red flags above are present.

Complication hierarchy – atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis is a red flag because embolic stroke risk rises sharply; the examiner expects you to link rhythm disturbance to the underlying valve lesion.

Coronary arterial tree – epicardial vessels, microvascular perfusion, subendocardial oxygen demand: Ischaemia reduces contractility and can precipitate decompensation; ECG changes or troponin rise are red‑flags.

ai.title: Red Flags in Clinical Medicine
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Red flags are clinical clues that signal potentially life‑threatening conditions or urgent complications. Recognising them guides immediate investigation, treatment and referral, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Red flags are specific signs, symptoms or test results that indicate a high probability of a serious underlying pathology requiring prompt action.
b: They are not exhaustive lists but decision points

sections.p: Severity is graded by the likelihood of imminent deterioration or death. Staging uses established scores (e.g., CURB‑65 for pneumonia, WHO‑SAGE for malaria).

In East Africa, common red‑flag causes include severe infections (TB, malaria, bacterial sepsis), cardiovascular emergencies (rheumatic heart disease, pulmonary embolism), and metabolic derangements (hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia).
b: Severe malaria with splenomegaly and anaemia

sections.p: Patients often report sudden onset, severe pain, or rapid decline. Physical exam may reveal focal tenderness, abnormal breath sounds, or altered mental status.
b: Chest pain + dyspnoea + tachycardia suggests pulmonary embolism

sections.p: Investigation choice depends on availability and red‑flag presence.

t.b: High WBC or low Hb signals urgent care
Positive test requires immediate antimalarial therapy
Absent in low‑resource settings; clinical judgement must guide referral
Low SpO₂ is a red flag for respiratory failure

sections.p: Red flags often herald complications such as sepsis, organ failure, or thromboembolism. Early recognition prevents progression.
b: Severe anaemia + tachycardia = risk of cardiac failure

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Drug choice considers efficacy, safety, and local availability.
After stabilization, arrange follow‑up to monitor recovery and prevent recurrence. Prevention focuses on vaccination, malaria prophylaxis, and early treatment of infections.
Many red‑flag conditions mimic benign illnesses. Distinguishing features are key.
b: Severe malaria can mimic dengue; look for splenomegaly and haemoglobinuria

sections.p: Some tests may be falsely normal or abnormal due to local factors. Clinicians must interpret in context.
b: HbA1c may be unreliable in sickle cell disease

faq.q: What is the most urgent red flag in a febrile patient?
faq.a: Hypoxaemia (SpO₂ <90%) indicates impending respiratory failure and requires immediate oxygen or ventilation.

faq.q: How do you differentiate severe malaria from dengue?
faq.a: Severe malaria shows splenomegaly, haemoglobinuria, and a positive rapid malaria test; dengue typically has haemorrhagic signs without splenomegaly.

faq.q: When is a chest X‑ray mandatory?
faq.a: If the patient has high fever, tachypnoea, or focal chest signs—these are red flags that warrant imaging even in low‑resource settings.

exam: A 28‑year‑old presents with fever, rigors, and haemoglobinuria. What is the next step? — Perform a rapid malaria test; a positive result mandates artesunate therapy.
A patient with chest pain and tachycardia is found to have a normal ECG. What red flag still warrants urgent care? — Hypoxaemia on pulse oximetry; SpO₂ <90% triggers oxygen therapy.
A child with severe anaemia (Hb 6 g/dL) is stable. What is the most important red flag to monitor? — Tachycardia >140 bpm indicating impending cardiac failure.

A patient with suspected pulmonary embolism has a normal Wells score but is haemodynamically unstable. What is the red flag? — Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) mandates immediate anticoagulation and possible thrombolysis.
A patient with suspected sepsis has a creatinine of 1.8 mg/dL. What red flag influences antibiotic choice? — Avoid nephrotoxic agents; prefer ceftriaxone over aminoglycosides.
A pregnant woman with fever and abdominal pain has a normal abdominal exam. What red flag should prompt imaging? — Persistent fever >39°C and tachycardia suggest ectopic pregnancy or appendicitis.

A patient with known rheumatic heart disease presents with new atrial fibrillation. What red flag indicates high stroke risk? — Atrial fibrillation in mitral stenosis increases embolic stroke risk; urgent anticoagulation is required.

A patient with suspected meningitis has a normal CSF opening pressure. What red flag still requires treatment? — Positive Gram stain or bacterial culture; treat empirically with ceftriaxone and dexamethasone.
